trace.claim: The paper argues that online political hostility is associated with political engagement and its antecedents, such as political interest, political knowledge, and participation, rather than being solely linked to deprivation, marginalization, or personality-based factors like the Dark Triad.

The paper argues against the idea that politically engaged users are only engaged in benign or constructive political discourse, suggesting instead that such engagement can lead to more polarized and antagonistic behavior.
The paper argues against the notion that online political hostility is limited to fringe or isolated users, by showing that hostile users are more active and have greater reach on X/Twitter.

The paper argues against the idea that affective polarization is merely a correlate of hostility, instead suggesting it may condition the relationship between political engagement and hostility by shaping emotional orientations toward political opponents.
Online political hostility is positively associated with indicators of political engagement and its antecedents, such as political interest, political knowledge, and online participation.
Politically hostile users on X/Twitter post more frequently, have more friends and followers, and thus have greater potential reach.

The study uses a dataset combining panel survey data with online behavioral data from X (formerly Twitter) to examine associations between online political hostility and indicators of political engagement.
The panel survey data includes measures of education, internal efficacy, political knowledge, political interest, and self-reported participation in both offline and online political activities.
The online behavioral data consists of 9,250,180 posts scraped from 2,567 panelists between March 2019 and January 2021.
The primary measure of online political hostility is based on a word embeddings approach called the Super-Unsupervised (SU) approach.
The SU approach calculates hostility scores by measuring the cosine similarity between individual posts and a combined 'political hate' word vector derived from political and hate-related terms.
The study includes a secondary robustness measure using the AFINN sentiment dictionary to assign sentiment scores to individual words.
The study includes a measure of affective polarization based on feeling thermometer ratings of three Republican and three Democratic political leaders.
The study controls for Big Five personality traits, party identification, age, gender, and income in its analyses.
The study uses a Random-Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Model (RI-CLPM) to analyze temporal within-person associations between political engagement and online political hostility.
Online political hostility is positively associated with political interest, political knowledge, and online participation.
Users with higher levels of affective polarization show stronger associations between political engagement and online political hostility.
Politically hostile users post more frequently and have more friends and followers, indicating greater activity and potential reach on X/Twitter.

The study finds that online political hostility is linked to political engagement and its antecedents, such as education and internal efficacy, beyond explanations based on deprivation or personality.
The paper does not establish a causal relationship between political engagement and online political hostility.
The paper does not claim that political engagement causes online political hostility.
The paper does not show that political engagement directly causes hostility in a one-way direction.
The paper does not demonstrate that the observed associations are due to time-varying confounding or reciprocal relationships.
The paper does not claim that the Big Five personality traits directly test personality-based accounts of online hostility.
The paper does not show that the observed patterns of hostility apply to all social media platforms.
The paper does not establish that users with high political hostility have formal network influence or are central in online communities.

The authors position their study within the classical theory of political engagement and extend it by examining the link between political engagement and online political hostility, arguing that such hostility is associated with engagement indicators rather than just deprivation or personality-based explanations.

The authors integrate findings from both socioeconomic and psychological perspectives on online hostility, using the classical framework of political engagement to provide a broader context for understanding the relationship between engagement and hostility.
The paper builds on the claim that affective polarization increases political engagement by suggesting it also intensifies online political hostility, rather than merely increasing participation.

The paper challenges the notion that online political hostility is primarily driven by personality-based traits like the Dark Triad, by emphasizing instead its connection to political engagement and its antecedents.
The paper disputes the claim that hostile political expression is limited to fringe audiences by showing that hostile users are more active and have greater reach on X/Twitter.
